subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, further to the urban goals set forth in the Speech from the Throne, I wish to inform the House today that the government is creating a $100 million urban demonstration program and fund to be administered through the Minister of State for Urban Affairs.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext:
This demonstration program is designed to foster projects that will find solutions to urban problems and demonstrate those solutions for adoption and implementation in all regions of Canada.
The fund applies to the five-year period from 1975-76 to 1980-81. It is a further indication of the clear determination of this government to meet the urban goals announced in the Speech from the Throne, and it will also provide a strong and imaginative foundation for Canada's full participation in the 1976 United Nations Conference-Exposition on Human Settlements to be held in Vancouver. I hope this conference will be known as Habitat 2000.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this $100 million fund will be used to support urban projects in many critical areas. We need to develop innovative projects to show the effective working of new methods of house design and house construction, to demonstrate the feasibility of new, low energy urban systems, to illustrate new ways of getting the utmost value from scarce and expensive natural resources by recycling for multiple use, and to apply new technology to many other critical areas such as improved
public transportation and arrangements for the financing, building and administration of new communities, or renewed communities.
The new fund is intended to launch a program of innovation in the urban field. It will apply to federal programs, provincial programs, and to programs developed by municipalities. It will also apply to projects put forward by the private sector and individual Canadians.
Innovation is a difficult thing to foster and support. This fund will be used to enable projects to embody desirable innovations that would not be possible without such additional support. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, it is not tied to any existing federal program but, rather, it can be used in a discretionary manner as opportunities and circumstances require.
Moreover, we intend to manage the program and fund so that the impact on innovation will be as pervasive as possible. I would hope that over the five years we can translate this initial $100 million into innovative projects valued at many times that figure.
It is difficult to say how many projects will be selected but I would hope that perhaps as many as 20 or more would be launched over the next two years. From those 20 or so projects, Mr. Speaker, a smaller number will be nominated as Canadian demonstration projects for inclusion in the United Nations conference. The program and fund will also be managed, of course, to ensure that all regions of the country share equitably in its benefits.
Proposals for demonstration projects can be put forward by federal departments and agencies, by provinces, by municipalities, by the private sector and by individual Canadians, including, I hope, as a result of the very keen interest of the members of this House. Proposals for projects should be sent to the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs, where a secretariat has been established to plan and implement Canada's participation in the United Nations conference.
In addition to interdepartmental and intergovernmental review the proposals will be subjected to a thorough evaluation of their potential effectiveness in solving urban problems and demonstrating solutions by a special committee which I have appointed to advise me on project selection. This group of experts is headed by Dr. Kenneth Hare of the University of Toronto and former president of the University of British Columbia.
This evaluation process, I should add, Mr. Speaker, will involve full consultation with other levels of governments, where necessary. Governments must press forward with immediate solutions employing existing methods and programs relating, for example, to housing and transportation. But we must also adopt measures to generate new approaches, to generate improved technology and innova-

tive solutions. That is the purpose of this program and of this announcement.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today the minister has announced a $100 million urban demonstration program-I emphasize the word "demonstration"-and fund to be administered by himself. He will be the czar of this demonstration. The program will extend over a five-year period, from 1975-76 to 1980-81. The object is not to build houses; the object is to provide a strong foundation for Canada's participation in a conference to be held in Vancouver sponsored by the United Nations, dealing with the question of human settlements.
No one has any complaint about or criticism of that conference. The minister wants the conference to be known as Habitat 2000. That is one of the problems with this program; it will be the year 2000 before the minister will be able to build any houses for the Canadian people.
On the second page of his announcement is the thrust of his novel suggestion, a suggestion made at a time when there is a national housing crisis in Canada. In addition, the latest figures for the cost of living have just come out and the cost of living has never been higher. From 1972 to 1973 the average increase in the cost of housing in Vancouver was 32 per cent, in Calgary 23.2 per cent and in Toronto 29 per cent.
In face of this crisis, Mr. Speaker, let us analyse this demonstration program, which I say is a lot of fluff. We would have other names for it out west, but it is just straight bluff. The minister called it a program of innovation. I wondered just what the word "innovation" meant so I checked. It means "a program of change from the established custom; a program to create a new thing or a new method". I think it is a program of inhalation, because the minister must have been sniffing glue to bring in a program of this kind.
Let us see what this great program of the Liberal party is going to do. It is going to develop innovative projects. It is going to create new methods of house design and construction and low energy urban systems. It is going to apply, whatever that means, new technology in many areas. But it is not going to build one new house in Canada. There is a low housing vacancy rate right across this country, .6 per cent. Here we are at a time when there is a real housing shortage in Toronto and Vancouver as well as in other cities; at the present time the vacancy rate in Toronto and Vancouver is less than one per cent. People must have housing, but we are presented instead with a program to spend $100 million over five years to demonstrate the good will of the minister at a time when we have a national housing crisis.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: The situation is chronic right across the land. Interest rates on first mortgages are 10 per cent to 12 per cent and on second mortgages 21 per cent, at a time when only 5 per cent of Canada's wage earners can afford to buy new houses in many cities. Yet the minister has decided now to present this bunch of bluff as a means of solving the national housing crisis.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext:
The only thing we lack is innovation in leadership. The only change that will bring about a new and effective housing program is a change of minister and, above all, a change of government.
I need not say more, Mr. Speaker, except-

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to see those hon. members go back to their home cities which are experiencing these high costs in housing and clap there as they are clapping now in the House of Commons.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: The United Nations is, of course, the world organization for peace and security. I am always pleased to see Canada participate in any conference, but at a time when there is no peace of mind, at a time when we should be declaring war on the national housing crisis, the government is setting up a bluff of $100 million. It is a joke.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the program announced by the government involves wrong spending at the wrong time and in a completely wrong area. The minister said in his statement that this is a "demonstration program designed to foster projects that will find solutions to urban problems", and that it will also provide the foundation for Canada's participation in the 1976 United Nations Conference to be held, incidentally, in the city of Vancouver.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: In his own riding.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext:
The minister said he wants this conference to be known as Habitat 2000. I suggest in all seriousness that all this program is going to mean is $100 million down the drain, of no help to people in meeting housing requirements in Canada.
Why do I say that, Mr. Speaker? First of all, the minister knows full well that under Part V of the National Housing Act his own department in the past few years has spent almost $100 million on grants for research and development. But what results have we seen from the expenditure of all that money on research and development? The first point to be made is that most of the information has not even been published. We have not had access to the studies that have been carried out by people in his department. Second, most of the studies that have been done have led to total inaction. We do not know what was in those studies, but we do know that they have not led to programs of any real significance produced by this minister. The most glaring example of the results of that research program is the Dennis report, a serious study of low income housing in Canada, but the minister did not have the decency to publish it and its conclusions did not come to light until the NDP got a copy and released it, following which the government produced a truncated version many weeks later.
March 13, 1974

We do not need more research at this time in respect of the problems of housing in urban Canada. If we do need more research and development it is in respect of the problems of housing in rural and northern Canada. That would be meaningful spending in terms of research and development. We have already been researched to death in terms of where 85 per cent of the population of Canada lives and do not need another dollar spent in that area.
I strongly suspect that the only reason-I will not say what I was about to say-that the government is spending $100 million in this area at this time is that the minister resides in the city of Vancouver. There is to be a conference there in 1976 and it will do him no political harm to pour lots of money into that area of the country. Otherwise, it is being spent to disguise the fact, in terms of urban Canada where 85 per cent of the people live, that no one will get a house in the next few years because the minister will say they are looking into that area and are going to come up with an imaginative new program.
I remind the minister of what happened in respect of Habitat. He says he hopes the conference will be known as Habitat 2000. What happened to Habitat in Montreal? I do not know how many millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money were spent on it. Who is living there now? Upper income Canadians. Those with very high salaries are living in that highly subsidized housing paid for by the majority of the taxpayers of Canada. That is what happened to Habitat in Montreal.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: We can do without that kind of example. We need action and not more studies on housing. I remind the minister that his home province of British Columbia has set aside $100 million for housing, $50 million to be used for land assembly and $40 million to subsidize mortgage rates. In contrast the federal government with all its resources is spending just a little more than $300 million. An amount of $100 million is being spent by one province with an NDP government and $300 million is being spent by this inactive Liberal government.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CREATION OF URBAN DEMONSTRATION PROGRAM AND FUND
speechtext:
The gentleman and lady on my right are doing some yelling. The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) concluded his statement with a criticism of the government but presented not one iota of a solution from the Conservative Party. All they do is criticize.
I conclude with this observation. What is needed is action in two areas of housing policy that affect Canadians. One is interest rates. The situation is the same in England and the Labour Party is now acting in that regard. We need to tell the banks to make money available at 6 per cent and frankly say: You are not going to make a profit in that area, but so what? People need housing and you can make a profit in other sections of your investments; we are going to get investment money for housing. That is one thing. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Stanbury (Minister of National Revenue):
maintopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACTS, 1867 TO 1965 PROVISION OF REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE FOR THE NORTHWEST TERRITORIES AND THE YUKON
subsubtopic: REVENUE FROM SALES TAX ON BUILDING MATERIAL
speechtext: In so far as National Revenue is concerned: The tax on building materials was introduced on June 14, 1963. However, revenue statistics were not available until 1967 when the general sales tax rate was changed to 12 per cent while the tax on the specific building materials listed in Schedule V of the Excise Tax Act remained at 11 per cent. The department was thus enabled to identify the revenue derived from the sale of those building materials taxable at the lesser rate. This was done until March 1972. At that time, in order to ease the tax accounting burden of taxpayers, the practice of having them report those taxes being paid at the 11 per cent rate separately from those being paid at the 12 per cent rate was discontinued. maintopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACTS, 1867 TO 1965 PROVISION OF REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE FOR THE NORTHWEST TERRITORIES AND THE YUKON
subsubtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext:
1. It is assumed that reference is being made to an adjudicatory claims commission. The government believes that negotiation is the preferred course, having regard to the nature of these claims. Negotiation fosters more direct involvement of those concerned and permits more comprehensive treatment of the issues. In his recommendations to date the Commissioner on Indian Claims, who is responsible for studying claims and facilitating the development of settlement processes, has proposed negotiation as the preferred course to be followed. Adjudicatory machinery may be necessary at some point for certain types of claims, but the government feels that it would be premature to deal with this possibility at this time. Neither Mr. Barber nor the government has so far encountered a situation in which the judgmental processes inherent in an adjudicatory claims commission seem necessary or desirable.
2. (a) Appropriate steps will be taken to ensure that terms of any settlement become public knowledge, (b) It is expected that settlements will vary to take into account the divergent circumstances on which claims are based. No doubt participants will want to feel that any settlement is comparable to others and this will be a factor in the government's approach to any proposals put before it.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to express a sense of urgency and shock with regard to the figures on the cost of living released today. In so doing, I would seek to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a special and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the announcement today by Statistics Canada that the January to February increase in the food index is the largest such increase in a quarter of a century.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   CONSUMER AFFAIRS INCREASE IN CONSUMER PRICE INDEX

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   CONSUMER AFFAIRS INCREASE IN CONSUMER PRICE INDEX
speechtext:
The hon. member for St. John's East has provided the written notice required by section 2 of Standing Order 26. As hon. members know, the Chair has always been reluctant to concur in the putting of a motion for the adjournment of the House on the basis of monthly statistics produced and provided by Statistics Canada. In
Motions for Papers
spite of the importance of the matter, I have the same reluctance today. The statistic on which the hon. member bases his proposed motion has reference to the matter of inflation which has been under discussion during much of the throne speech debate. The subamendment moved by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) was concerned with the problem of inflation.

It is my intention today to outline the major provisions of the bill mainly in general terms. While I would be happy to answer questions and points raised by hon. members to the extent I have the opportunity to do so during the course of this debate, I look forward to the committee study of the bill where there would be an even greater opportunity for me to deal with hon. members' questions, ideas and suggestions and to discuss these with them, as well as all the various proposals of the bill, in full detail.
This bill reflects the view that all Canadians can benefit from having a marketplace subject to the stimulus and the pressures of the forces of competition. However, it places particular emphasis on measures to assist them as consumers and also as small businessmen. A fundamental necessity for consumers, if they are to operate successfully in a market system, is the availability of full and accurate information about the goods and service that are offered to them for sale. Therefore, the bill proposes to make considerably stronger and clearer the sections of our present competition law, the Combines Investigation Act, dealing with misleading advertising. The new bill forbids
March 13, 1974

the making of a representation to the public that is false or misleading in any material respect.
As the House may know, this is a broader coverage than in the present law which applies largely to published advertisements. The bill would define a representation to the public as including anything imprinted on or attached to the article offered for sale, expressed on a point of purchase display or on display advertising. In fact, it would also include statements made by the salesmen. In addition, the bill would make clear that a representation may be misleading, and therefore forbidden by it, equally because of the general impression it conveys as much as from its literal meaning. But one can well argue that even full and accurate information about goods and services offered is not sufficient for consumers when those products, and often those services, more and more frequently involve advanced and complex technology beyond the knowledge and understanding of most people today. Therefore, I believe the consumer today must have greater assurance than is the case at present concerning the basic standard of performance to be reasonably expected from the product or service in question.
This, I think, means improving and strengthening our laws on warranties and guarantees. Much of this area falls within the provincial jurisdiction, pertaining as it does to the law of contract. However, the federal government also has jurisdiction in this area and has proposed in Bill C-7 new protection in this field using this jurisdiction to deal with the deceptive and misleading aspects of warranties and guarantees. I think these proposals should complement any provincial reforms which eventually would come in this area. They would at the very least provide some basic form of protection for consumers across the country irrespective of the extent the province in which they live may or may not come to update its law in this regard.
The bill therefore proposes that it would be an offence to make a representation to the public in a form that purports to be a warranty or guarantee of a product that is materially misleading. It proposes that it would be an offence to offer a warranty or guarantee if there is no reasonable prospect that it would be carried out. Any warranty or guarantee that limits the supplier's liability to a standard lower than that which would apply under the civil law would be deemed to be materially misleading unless the fact that it is limited in this way is clearly stated in it. Also, warranties that confer no material advantage on the purchaser would be considered misleading in a material respect, and therefore contrary to the proposed bill.
The bill would also prohibit under criminal sanction a number of selling practices if they are carried out as defined in the bill. I think it could be said there has developed a commonalty of view about them that they should not be allowed in these forms in the marketplace. These practices are: referred selling, pyramid selling, bait and switch selling, double-ticketing and sale above advertised price, and I propose to discuss them in full and complete detail when the bill is before the appropriate standing committee.
Competition Bill
Another necessity for the effective operation of the marketplace is that arrangements and agreements between sellers do not deprive consumers and businessmen as well of the benefits of competition with respect to such things as price, quality and range of products available. Bill C-7 would strengthen the government's ability to deal with collusive agreements in restraint of trade by redefining the test that must be met in order to prove that such agreements are contrary to the law. The present law states that for an agreement to be contrary to it, it must be proven that the agreement prevents or lessens competition unduly. But in some cases in recent years the courts have interpreted the word "unduly" to mean the complete or virtual elimination of competition in the relevant market. In other cases, the courts have disagreed with such a demanding interpretation.
In any event, cases can and do arise in which competition is lessened to an extent that is obviously detrimental to the public but which might not meet the severity of the test of complete or virtual elimination of competition. The bill proposes, therefore, that in order to prove that an agreement prevents or lessens competition unduly, it would not be necessary to establish complete or virtual elimination of competition in the relevant market. In other words, the amendment would make clear to the courts that parliament does not intend the more rigorous interpretation, which has been a matter of argument in the courts for some years, to be the one to be applied.
Let me turn to another matter important to the development of law whose purpose is helping to ensure the effective operation of the marketplace in the interest of the consumer and of all Canadians. This is the extent to which that law in fact applies to activities carried out in the marketplace. At the present time, our competition law, the Combines Investigation Act, does not apply to services, aside from a few limited exceptions. Yet the service sector comprises some 20 per cent of our gross domestic product. The bill, therefore, would extend our competition law to cover services generally. I think this is a major step forward in the development and putting in place of competition policy in Canada. The bill itself mentions some limited exceptions, but one basic exception to this coverage would be with respect to those activities authorized or regulated by other valid federal or provincial laws.
This exception is not stated in the bill itself but arises out of existing jurisprudence. The effect of this jurisprudence, taken together with the proposals in the bill, would mean that all economic activity in Canada would be subject to some form of social control on behalf of the public, either through federal competition law or through other specific provincial or federal legislation. If a sector is taken out of the purview of competition law through being placed under another law of a regulatory nature, I think it can be said that this means in effect that the Canadian people, through their elected representatives at the provincial or federal level, have decided that this form of social control is more desirable and more in their over-all interest than the form made possible through competition policy.
Turning to another matter, the bill would make bid rigging, that is, the practice of entering into agreements to

March 13, 1974
Competition Bill
refrain from bidding on tenders or submitting tender prices arrived at by collusion, to be an offence without further proof of the intention or effect of this practice.
Also, the present law regarding resale price maintenance would be strengthened by the bill. Resale price maintenance keeps selling prices higher than they would otherwise be by eliminating competition at wholesale and retail levels. One of the ways the bill strengthens the present law is to make it an offence not simply to require a customer to resell a product at a specific price but to make any attempt to influence upward or discourage the reduction of a price.
The bill also strengthens the rules for competition in the banking industry but proposes that their application be the responsibility of the Inspector General of Banks.
The bill deals with a number of trade practices which under certain circumstances could be acceptable but not in others and which could have detrimental effects, again depending on the circumstances. The practices dealt with in the bill are: refusal to deal, consignment selling, exclusive dealing, tied sales, and market restriction. Such practices could, under certain circumstances, be used to prevent the free operation of market forces and limit the consumers' choice. They have been the cause of many complaints to the combines branch, particularly from smaller businessmen who feel they have been restricted in their business activities on the part of suppliers or would-be suppliers. But, the present law does not cover these particular practices.
Under the bill, the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission would be given the power to issue orders forbidding or modifying these practices. These orders would have the same effect as orders of a civil court and they could be made by the commission following hearings on particular situations brought before it by the director of the combines branch. The bill also proposes that failure to comply with such an order would be grounds for a criminal prosecution.
The sections setting out matters reviewable by the commission make provision to protect the rights of the parties against whom an order is sought. Each practice is defined, as are the conditions under which an order may be made in each situation. Moreover, before any order can be issued, anyone against whom an order is sought in the words of the bill, "must be afforded a reasonable opportunity to be heard." These words in the act, when read together with the Federal Court Act to which I will refer in a moment, are intended to cover such matters as the right of the person against whom an order is sought to know the case against him, the right to call evidence to answer it, the right to cross-examine and the right to appear in person and be represented by counsel or otherwise.
Appeals from decisions of the commission will be provided by the Federal Court Act to the appeal division of the Federal Court where the commission failed to observe a principle of natural justice or otherwise acted beyond or refused to exercise its jurisdiction, where it erred in law in making its decision or order, or where it based its decision or order on an erroneous finding of fact that it made in a perverse or capricious manner or without regard for the material before it.

One very important proposal in the bill, in my view, is that the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission be given the jurisdiction to make orders to forbid the implementation in Canada of foreign judgments, laws or directives where it found them to be contrary to the Canadian public interest. This would include such matters as their effects on Canadian trade and industry. The bill proposes that the director of the combines branch would have authority to bring such situations before the commission, and where the orders are not obeyed this would be grounds for criminal prosecution.
I think that recent events have demonstrated the importance of this proposal and have provided a strong argument for the House to make a favourable decision on this bill at the earliest possible date.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, ADMINISTRATION AND OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, ADMINISTRATION AND OFFENCES
speechtext:
Let me go on to say that the benefits of the proposals in a bill like the one now before the House, in my view can become meaningful only to the extent that there is improvement in the procedures and remedies available for their application and enforcement.
Here, too, I believe the bill would bring about positive change. The bill calls for the Attorney General of Canada and the provincial attorneys general to be given the power to seek interim injunctions to prevent the repetition or continuation of alleged offences against the act until the main issues are settled by the courts. This would be a completely new procedure in so far as competition law in Canada is concerned.
Equally new is the proposal that anyone injured by a violation of the act would be able to sue for full damages and costs. As I have said previously, I believe that to be meaningful this right should be exercisable not only by an individual citizen or government but also by citizens as a group through class or representative actions.
It is my hope that the bill in the form in which it is finally approved by parliament will enable class actions to take place for damages caused by violations of it, in so far as the federal parliament has the authority to make such a decision. As also I have said previously, I have already asked officials of my department and of the Department of Justice to explore what further drafting may be required to accomplish this important objective.
The bill also contains proposals that could well lead to a speeding up of the bringing to trial and disposition of cases dealing with competition matters. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the present law states that such cases can be brought either in the provincial courts or in the Federal Court, but in order to bring such cases in the Federal Court the consent of the accused must first be obtained. The new bill proposes that where the accused is a corporation it would not be necessary for the Crown first to obtain its consent in order to bring a case under our competition law to the Federal Court. It also proposes that trials could be held either in the place of residence of the individual or company involved or in the place where the offence was committed. These proposals, I think, would enable the Crown to have regard to the volume of work
March 13, 1974

already pending in a particular court before deciding where to launch a certain proceeding.
Hon. members will have noted that the proposals in the bill are cast in the form of amendments to the existing Combines Act and not as a complete replacement for it. This, I submit, will make easier to apply and will make more immediately effective this first part of the government's program to modernize our competition law.
I would also submit that the bill deals not only with matters of direct and current concern to consumers and small businessmen but also proposes important changes in broader areas of competition policy which are applicable to large as well as small companies.
I think this is demonstrated by what I have said about such matters as the extension of the total purview of our competition law to services, the change in the definition of the term "unduly", as well as giving the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission the authority to review certain kinds of business practices.
What, then, remains for the second stage of competition policy? I think it could be said that generally speaking there is a need to develop legislation containing additional criteria and methods upon which to judge mergers, monopolies and specialization agreements. These, although they may be restrictive of competition, could on balance be in the public interest through their effects on efficiency and productivity, depending on the particular circumstances involved.
There have been many arguments made that there are circumstances where the criminal law approach alone should not be used, but instead there should be a way of applying statutory tests to determine what the effects of a proposed merger would be on competition and efficiency. If the tests are not met, it could be argued that there should be a procedure for dealing with the transaction by appropriate remedial orders.
Certainly a high priority will have to be given in stage II to provisions which will enable competition law to play its part in helping improve the efficiency of Canadian business and its ability to compete abroad. In the bill to implement stage I which is now before the house it is proposed that the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission be given new jurisdiction to review and, in certain circumstances, to make remedial orders about certain kinds of trade practices. Another aim for stage II is to decide what other trade practices should be made subject to review in the same way.
Among the practices which we are looking at are interlocking directorates, delivered pricing, reciprocal buying, quantity discounts, and loss leaders. Their effects may vary depending upon the circumstances, and these practices, I think, are candidates for handling in the same way as are the trade practices covered in stage I, that is, initially by a civil approach rather than by a criminal one so that under proper circumstances the economy would not be deprived of what could be instruments useful for competitive purposes.
As I have said, I think we should consider whether general jurisdiction in the trade practices area should and could be created at the federal level similar to that exercised by the Federal Trade Commission in the United
Competition Bill
States. This body, as the House may know, in addition to having jurisdiction to prohibit or modify specific activities has broad authority to prohibit unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices generally in the marketplace. It has authority to issue cease and desist orders under threat, initially, of civil penalties and to issue guidelines with respect to practices in a specific industry or with respect to certain kinds of practices, irrespective of the industry in which they are found.
I have said previously that one argument for the federal government using a general approach in the general trade practices area would be that it would be done on a national basis and would therefore help bring about a useful degree of uniformity across the country. I have argued that this would avoid a multiplicity of possibly overlapping and confronting rules, and thereby facilitate Canadian economic activity.
All that I have said so far underscores the necessity in stage II of making decisions on appropriate institutions and procedures to enable any possible policy changes of the kind I have mentioned to be carried out fairly and effectively. Decisions in this area are another objective of the second stage of competitions policy. By having the areas which I have just mentioned, particularly those dealing with mergers and specialization agreements, dealt with in the second stage of competition legislation, I think there can be greater certainty that this will be consistent with the government's evolving industrial policies and its foreign investment policy. At the same time, by asking the House to deal now with Bill C-7 I am taking action on behalf of the government to enable parliament to take decisions earlier than would otherwise be the case in some important areas particularly relevant to present public concerns linked with current inflationary pressures.
Let me now take a moment to pay tribute to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) and to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) for their efforts which helped lead to the bill now before the House.
In conclusion I want to say that the proposals in Bill C-7 to implement the first stage of the government's new competition policy, as well as the proposals to come in the second stage of policy development will, I submit, result in legislation which will at one and the same time help bring about a more efficient and productive Canadian economy, and help provide expanded consumer protection in a marketplace characterized by high technology and massive organization of production and distribution. I therefore urge the House to give second reading to this bill as quickly as possible so that it can go at the earliest possible stage to committee for detailed but, I hope, speedy consideration and decision.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, ADMINISTRATION AND OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, ADMINISTRATION AND OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with mixed feelings that our party joins this debate on major amendments to the Combines Investigation Act. On the one hand we are glad that the government has finally learned its lesson after the debacle it created with its infamous Bill C-256, the competition act, in the twenty-eighth parliament. The bill before us today represents a rejection of the omnibus nature of the earlier proposal,

March 13, 1974
Competition Bill
and it rightfully proceeds in an incremental fashion. It is in a form which is more manageable in size and is less radical in its philosophical and legislative thrust. Also, I think there are practical advantages to bringing in this scaled-down competition policy as an amendment to the existing act, as opposed to introducing a brand new act.
We are also pleased that the government appears to be giving some priority to the consumer protection aspects of competition policy, a course of action strongly recommended by PC members of the Special Committee on Trends in Food Prices last spring, which recommendation eventually found its way into the first report of that committee. I suppose that if this government is going to do nothing to try to stop inflation, the very least it can do for consumers is to provide some means of redress against the misleading or unfair practices of unscrupulous merchants in the marketplace.
I said we approach this debate with mixed feelings. On the negative side, we are rather puzzled by the sudden haste of the government in introducing a bill of this magnitude and importance on a Monday and rushing it into second reading on a Wednesday, two days later. The legislation involves fundamental philosophical considerations of a political, legal, economic and federal-provincial nature. It creates, to all intents and purposes, a new, highly centralized agency which has the potentiality of interposing itself into a major segment of Canadian political and economic life. Affecting matters within both federal and provincial jurisdiction, the bill will permit the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission to alter or restructure market distribution systems in Canada in an unprecedented fashion.
The point is that this bill, in its substantive impact, is no minor tinkering or legislative patchwork job. It is major legislation and deserves careful scrutiny and a full and informed debate, not only by members of this House but by the many businessmen, consumer groups and provincial governments who will be directly affected by its provisions.
I want to make it clear to the minister that it is the position of our party that persons, associations or provincial governments wanting time to study and analyse this bill should have it in order that meaningful briefs can be presented to the standing committee to which it is referred. We would suggest that a minimum period of some four to six weeks prior to commencement of committee hearings might be in order to permit this study, analysis and preparation, fully acknowledging of course that this bill is identical in form to the one the minister introduced on November 5, 1973.
A more important reason for our mixed reactions to this bill relates to the main reason why the bill was probably brought on in such haste. That is the shocking revelation over the past few weeks of the apparent inability of the Canadian government to protect Canadian economic sovereignty, as was so clearly evidenced by the almost aborted sale of Canadian locomotives to Cuba by MLW-Worth-ington Limited of Montreal. Members will recall that the company is a United States subsidiary carrying on business in Canada but which felt bound by the provisions of

the United States trading with the enemy act. That foreign law would have prohibited the sale to Cuba.
Obviously, the minister has felt compelled to bring in the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act because they contain provisions granting powers to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission to review instances where foreign judgments, foreign laws or directives from foreign managers are contrary to the Canadian public interest and, after according full opportunity to be heard, to make orders forbidding their implementation in Canada. As indicated by my leader on several occasions in this House last week, we agree with the goal of this legislative provision. It is obviously designed to prevent another MLW-Worthington situation from occuring.
Yet let us examine what the bill before us actually does in this area. Decisions which can have a fundamental policy impact on relations between sovereign countries, and adversely affect Canada's foreign trade or external relations, are delegated to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. Who ever heard of it before this bill was introduced? The government, wrongfully in my view, will be abdicating its own responsibilities to make policy decisions of this magnitude. We would strongly urge that the government reconsider vesting decisions of this sort in the Commission and consider vesting these decisions in the governor in council, in the same fashion that it does in making decisions to reduce tariffs or in making decisions respecting "significant benefit" under the Foreign Investment Review Act.
It would be all right for the RTPC to make recommendations to cabinet, but let us not have any abdication of responsibility on fundamental questions of economic policy. The Canadian public are entitled to know what the government of Canada will do about the implementation of a foreign law or directive that may affect our external trade or relations. The government should take the responsibility and not pass the buck to the RTPC.
What are the dangers of allowing the government to abdicate its responsibility in this area of fundamental policy? One has to refer only to the speech last Thursday of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) in the throne speech debate to see a graphic example of what I mean. In explaining to the House why he had been unable to pursue any real transportation policy as Minister of Transport, the minister gave this little anecdote:
Hon. members may say, "You are the minister: you do it." I have a few answers to that, Mr. Speaker. It is true that hon. members gave responsibilities to the minister, but they forgot to give any authority at all in many instances ... I told you I would not make a political speech. I am just trying to tell you the facts. Everything is done the same way. We have the CTC, which has final authority over almost everything, except in a few cases where there is provision for an appeal to the minister.
That explains the whole problem. The government must not be allowed to abdicate its responsibility to a subordinate agency and then come back and tell the Canadian people that it does not have the power to pursue a policy which it considers necessary.
Now let us move on and look at some of the other powers granted to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. The most far reaching power granted to the RTPC is to review instances of refusals to sell a product and to order a supplier to supply, or to recommend tariff
March 13, 1974

changes. At first blush this power seems disarmingly simple and reasonable. But upon further examination one can see that its practical implementation may have a radical impact on the nature of distribution systems for products in Canada which may well be inconsistent with the real economic and structural facts of life in this country.
The provision effectively will put the onus on the seller to justify his distribution system when he is called before the commission. That will likely be the general approach since the act invites the imposition of sanctions if the commission finds that the reason for inability of the person to obtain adequate supplies of the product is "an inadequate degree of competition in the market". There is no onus on the Director of Investigation and Research who brings the initial application to prove the inadequate degree of competition. Clearly, there is an open invitation for the commission merely to find it. The conclusion that refusal to sell is synonymous with inadequate competition may be too inviting for the commission under these circumstances.
But perhaps even more important than this reversal of the onus of proof is that this section represents a denial of the fundamental right of any seller to deal with whomsoever he wants. Not only does this right have a solid foundation in the common law of English jurisprudence, but the American legislation, with all its sophisticated provisions, clearly has no restrictions of this nature. Neither was any such restriction ever considered by congress when the legislation was last amended. Yet in that country, discount selling, which apparently is the aim of the minister in proposing the power for Canada, is flourishing to a far greater extent than in this country.
From the manufacturers' and distributors' point of view, taking away their right to refuse to sell in Canada would have a huge impact on their existing marketing systems of distribution. The provision also raises serious questions for various franchise systems, the practice of private branding, offshore suppliers and technical servicing requirements. These are matters of detailed substance which will have to be explored at the committee stage of this bill. One would hope that the minister might provide a fuller explanation of what he is trying to achieve and how he justifies the means that he has adopted. Also, one would hope there would be some explanation as to why this provision permits the commission to single-out one supplier for attention rather than merely authorize an order of general application to be applied to all suppliers in the same position.
There are also problems of procedure with the powers that are granted to the RTPC over refusals to sell, exclusive dealing practices, tied sales, market restrictions, etc. The minister very ably went through some of the procedural problems and provided some of the answers. While the act does specify that in the exercise of these powers the parties affected must be given "a reasonable opportunity to be heard", and that is a matter subject to judicial review in the Federal Court, the commission is left to make its own rules for the regulation of its proceedings and the performance of its duties and functions under the act. This may well lead to uncertainty and possible arbitrariness in proceedings before the commission, problems
Competition Bill
which might otherwise be overcome through specifying certain minimum procedural protections in the legislation itself. That is the drafting approach we would favour.
For example, the act is silent as to a right of reasonable notice of the hearing, the right to call and examine witnesses and to cross-examine other witnesses, the right to reasonable adjournments of the hearing and the right to a written decision with reasons. Perhaps more important as a practical matter is the silence of the act on the extent to which a party to be affected by an order of the commission will have access to and advance notice of the research done by the commission's staff in preparation for the hearing. With respect to a hearing on a refusal to sell application, for example, a manufacturer or distributor would want to have some advance information as to the concentration ratios the commission would be likely to adopt as its test for determining who is the dominant seller supplying goods in conditions of "inadequate degree of competition."
Even more important is the relationship of the commission research staff to the commissioners who will, after all, be making judicial and quasi-judicial decisions on many of the applications before them. In order to maintain the decision-making integrity of the commission in a quasi-judicial context, should not the commission's staff be attached to the Director of Research and Investigation, who makes the initial application, instead of the commission in order to guarantee fairness and the appearance of fairness?
Finally, it is our view that the standing committee giving clause by clause study to this bill should examine carefully whether there is need for a substantive right of appeal to the courts from an order of the RTPC. It is acknowledged that sections 18 and 28 of the Federal Court Act provide a comprehensive right of review of commission decisions made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis. The minister is quite in error when he calls it a right of appeal. I hope the minister will provide the rationale for the sufficiency of this review right in light of the recommendations in many of the briefs already submitted for a broader right of appeal.
One of the significant and more desirable aspects of the bill before us today is the application of many of the prohibitions of the act to service industries. This obviously has been included as a result of a very strong recommendation of the Economic Council of Canada in its interim report on competition policy released in August, 1969. The importance of this change is demonstrated by the fact that service activities previously not subject to the prohibitions of the act make up approximately 20 per cent of the gross domestic product of Canada.
There are various classes of service industries which are exempted for one reason or another. The largest, most important class of exemption is service activities which will be covered by laws, usually of a province or municipality, which regulate or authorize them. For reasons not entirely clear, the minister has not specifically included the exemption in the provisions of the bill but has taken the position that it flows from judicial interpretation.
486

March 13, 1974
Competition Bill
The minister points out that following the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act reference to the Supreme Court of Canada in 1957 it was held that regulatory schemes based on valid legislation, whether federal or provincial, could not be held to be "to the detriment of or against the interests of the public", as the then Combines Investigation Act put it, nor could they be schemes "to unduly limit or prevent competition" within the meaning of the then section 411 of the Criminal Code. This class of exemption will include services such as the professions, telephone companies and other forms of communication, and electrical power industries. They will all continue to enjoy immunity from combines prosecutions to the extent that their activities are specifically regulated or authorized by law.
We seriously question whether the reliance on judicial interpretation is really the right way to go about providing this class of exemption. As a practical matter, it will create uncertainties for various service industries which will be unable to determine whether their pricing practices are exempt from the federal prohibitory net. The securities industry is a case in point. While the bill specifically exempts bond and stock underwritings and primary distribution by groups of investment houses acting together in order to spread the risk, it is silent as to the rates of commission charged by brokers on the purchase or sale of listed or unlisted securities. The commission rates on all listed shares are set by the by-laws of the stock exchange which are subject to review and approval of the provincial securities commission in most cases.
On the one hand, it may be argued that because the bill specifically exempts bond and stock underwriting and primary distribution, then by implication it would include within the net of its prohibitions agreements as to its commission rates. Yet there is a 1907 judicial precedent, King V. Gage, holding that the by-laws of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange were not an undue restraint on trade and therefore exempt from federal combines law. However, that precedent would apply only to commodities regulated by the exchange which would not include unlisted shares traded by brokerage houses, the commission rate for which is generally agreed on as a matter of practice.
The practice of leaving the matter of judicial interpretation not only flies in the face of the normal doctrine of paramountcy, but it leaves quite an unacceptable and uncertain result for service industries wanting to know where they stand. In this regard, reference should be made to the remarks of Professor Bruce MacDonald of Queen's law school, an expert in the combines field, in an article in the 1969 Canadian Bar Review. I quote:
It may be that the courts, in refusing to apply the doctrine of paramountcy in favour of the Combines Investigation Act over provincial regulatory legislation, have achieved a politically viable solution. But when political accommodation is dependent upon a legal solution formulated by the courts, completely satisfactory results are fortuitous.
I suggest that the minister give consideration to providing a specific clause outlining the nature of this exemption for activities subject to special regulation. Clause 92 of Bill C-256, the competition act, in the last parliament attempted to do this, and I think a clause along these lines would be preferable to the form of the act before us today. In this way, service industries could have a much clearer

indication of whether their activities violated the act and whether they required special provincial legislation to legitimize their situation. I would mention, in particular, real estate agencies, advertising agencies, optometrists and telephone answering services which will find the situation somewhat unclear and which, along with the investment houses, would be assisted by a more specific clause.
I also want to indicate support for the clause of the bill providing that proclamation of the law in relation to agreements in restraint of trade in the service sector may be brought into force at a later date than the remainder of this legislation. This is necessary, obviously, to permit a reasonable time for the service sector to modify its practices in the light of the new provisions, or for them to be covered by valid provincial legislation, a process which takes a considerable period of time.
There are other specific exemptions of service industries which we find puzzling. For example, no rationale has been given for the exemption of collective bargaining activities. We think it is high time in Canada that the government applied anti-combines laws to the labour unions. We wonder whether it is the government's present coalition arrangement with another party in this House that prevents them from moving in that direction. Last September 20, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave an interview to Anthony Westell of the Toronto Star in which the right hon. gentleman said this:

We accept that big business and big unions are monopoly type powers that can be the cause of certain types of cost-push inflation, and we acted to counter that. The main thrust of our competition act didn't pass in the last parliament, but we said in the Speech from the Throne that we are going to reintroduce it in a different form. The main thrust still will be to counteract that monopolistic power. It will be to restore competition so that big businesses, monopolies, oligopolies will not be able to keep prices up or wages low because they have such a large hold on the market.
I intend, as Prime Minister, to counter that type of monopoly. I would include eventually the monopoly of labour in some of the large unions. But as you will see from our bill, as you saw from the last one, we are dealing first with the monopoly of business because that is the more dangerous one ... having dealt with that, if we are successful, we may also act in other laws to deal with the monopoly of labour.
Well, let me tell the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, that we think the government should deal with the monopoly of labour in some of the large unions right now, in the context of the bill which is before us.
Another curious exemption is the banks. While the bill creates minor amendments to the Bank Act dealing with agreements as to service charges, the amounts or kinds of loans or services, or persons to whom the loans or services will be made, we believe the minister should at least provide an acceptable rationalization as to why the banks should continue to be treated differently, under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Finance. This is a different and softer type of combines regime than exists for other financial institutions such as the trust companies and insurance companies.
The banks in this country, while they have been prosperous and efficient, have never been noted for their competitiveness. This is only too well known by small Canadian businessmen unable to secure adequate financ-
March 13, 1974

ing for their proposed business activities. Perhaps at the next ten-year review of the Bank Act there will be time to consider this question. In the meantime, I hope the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) will provide an acceptable rationale for their exemption from the present bill, at least something better than has been contained in the flurry of documents emanating from his office over the past few months.
Now, going back to the consumer protection provisions dealing with such matters as misleading advertising, bait and switch selling, untrue or misleading warranties or pyramid selling, it is in this area that we have the fewest differences of opinion with the government. However, there are a few matters of principle which give us cause for concern and which we would like the minister to consider prior to the committee stage of the bill. For example, on the misleading advertising provisions, why has the government eliminated the defence of mens rea or honest mistake by the merchant or advertiser prosecutions under those sections? In moving from the "credulous man" test to the "general impression" test, why did the government consider it necessary in section 36(5) to insert a "literal meaning" test as well? Why has the government sought to exempt printers and publishers from misleading advertising prosecutions, but not broadcasters? Should they not all be liable to prosecution if what they print, publish or broadcast is materially false or misleading?
To what extent, if any, has there been consultation with provincial governments which, after all, have power to introduce their own legislation on warranties and testimonials, pyramid and referral selling, bait and switch selling, and so on. What assurances can the minister give us that the legislation will not duplicate or conflict with provincial legislation, thus causing uncertainty and confusion for those in the marketplace? It is significant in this respect that the minister, upon introducing Bill C-227 on November 5 last, told us that he planned some form of provincial consultation after the bill had received second reading and been referred to committee. This was certainly a presumptuous posture on his part, indicating that he wanted to establish a parliamentary toe-hold as a bargaining tactic before approaching the provinces.
This, surely, is not the way to conduct federal-provincial relations; I would have thought that the government, as a result of its experiences in the field of energy, would by now have learned its lesson. This subtle but gradual erosion of provincial powers through unilateral extension of the criminal law is inimical to most provincial governments and it is about time the federal government started consulting and co-ordinating in the consumer area, rather than confronting and cajoling.
As a general proposition, and speaking personally, I am inclined to support the section of the bill bringing professional and amateur sports within the ambit of the Combines Investigation Act in the same way as other services, with the exception of specified arrangements among member clubs of the same sporting leagues. The commercial exploitation of young Canadian athletes has been going on for too long now, particularly in professional and amateur hockey.
We want to take a close look in committee at the provisions which purport to take into account the need for
Competition Bill
clubs to agree on arrangements for maintaining a balance among teams in their own league, particularly as this may affect many local amateur baseball and hockey leagues throughout Canada which could not survive without this sort of guarantee. At the same time, as the government moves in this direction it might consider ways and means by which a portion of the large signing bonuses paid to coming young professionals might be returned to the communities which developed their playing abilities, for the promotion and maintenance of the amateur leagues there as well as for the further development of young players there.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
There ought to be some sort of economic return when those young players come along and hit the big time, and I believe the government should give us a commitment that they will do something about it. I am pleased to see the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) in his place. I cannot help but wonder why the sections promoting competition in professional sports could not somehow have been brought to the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare who is blatantly seeking to protect the monopoly of the Canadian Football League against the competitive threat to the Toronto franchise of the World Football League. It is a sorry spectacle to see one minister of this government promoting competition and another, in the same week, seeking to deny it. Perhaps the Prime Minister might reconcile these ideological differences of opinion and clear up the confusion.
The bill before us provides important new civil remedies for persons who have suffered loss or damage resulting from a violation of the act or an order of the commission or a court, together with his full costs. Under the previous competition act, Bill C-256, there was provision for double damages, but the government has now wisely concluded that this was overreaching. The bill also provides that, for the first time, the courts will be able to issue interim injunctions to prevent the commission or continuation of suspected offences against the act until the main issue is disposed of. In many practical business situations this protection is even more important than the right to recover damages, because it allows victims of anti-competitive practices to take immediate action to protect themselves, pending ultimate court adjudication.
I thought the minister was really becoming quite bold when on February 2, in a speech he made in Toronto, he recognized the necessity for civil damage suits through class or representative actions. He said at that time:
It is my hope... that the bill in the form in which it is finally approved will enable class actions to take place for damages caused by violations of it, insofar as the federal parliament has the authority to make such decisions. I have therefore asked officials of the combines branch under the Department of Justice to explore what further drafting may be required to accomplish this important objective. Of course, it may well be unlikely (and here I am not expressing a final opinion) that the federal parliament will have the power to authorize class actions in those courts whose procedures are determined by provincial authorities. However, the bill proposes that the right to sue for damages which I have mentioned can be exercised not only in the provincial courts, but in the federal courts as well. And, I would presume that the federal parliament would have authority to deal with procedures to be used in a court created under federal law.
