Well, Mr. Speaker, some time between February 2 and last Monday the minister lost his nerve, for unfortunately we see no class action provisions in the new bill that he has brought forward. I sincerely hope that his courage returns by the time the bill is discussed in committee.
As for the criminal penalties in the bill, the government has apparently learned its lesson and is no longer trying to bludgeon the business community to death as it did with its $1 million and $2 million fines in the earlier bill, and the invidious section which presumed directors liable for offences of which the corporation had been convicted, which was really a denial of the due process of law.
However, by leaving the maximum fine under this bill at $10,000 with an alternative or supplement of imprisonment for one year, there may be the danger that the courts will be invited, perhaps to an excessive extent, to make use of the imprisonment section for serious contraventions of the act. I would prefer to see the maximum monetary fine increased to, say, $25,000 both as a move away from imprisonment as a means of regulating the economy, and in recognition of the fact that a monetary fine must on occasion be sufficiently high in order that it does not become just a licence fee as the price of continuing illegal activities.
There are many more problems with this bill which will undoubtedly come to light in the course of discussions in committee and as a result of the submissions that I know will come forward from consumer groups, business groups and from provincial governments. The far reaching powers to be granted to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission will require the closest scrutiny both as to substantive standards and as to matters of procedure. Throughout the complex legislative process that lies ahead in which the government seeks to grant new powers of intervention in business, to create a new agency, and to set up new standards of business behaviour, it will be good discipline for a member involved in the process to ask himself from time to time whether all the provisions of the legislation are really necessary, given the economic and structural facts of life in Canada today. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that members on this side of the House will ask themselves that question from time to time, and that will be our pragmatic approach as we assess each area of regulation.
As for the minister's purported second stage of his competition policy dealing with industrial restructuring, mergers, monopolies and specialization agreements, let me simply say that he should proceed with extreme caution. My colleagues on this side of the House will have more to say on this later in the debate.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, ADMINISTRATION AND OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my party I offer this bill a qualified welcome. I think it is a useful piece of legislation, by and large, so far as it goes. I agree with the decision of the government to proceed with this phase of the competition policy about which it has talked for some time. Meanwhile, we await the second, and in my judgment more important, phase that the government suggests will be along before the end of the year.

However, I want to say at this point that I do not agree that we need to wait that long for the second stage of the competition bill. Just because we move now to consider the implications of the legislation before us does not mean that there is any good reason to delay stage two. I therefore begin by urging the government to accelerate its schedule and to introduce the second stage of its competition policy at an earlier target date than it now appears to plan.
I should like to make one or two comments on the remarks made by my hon. friend from St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey). I do not fault the government for its haste in bringing in this bill on a Wednesday, having first introduced it on Monday. It is, of course, the same bill that was introduced in this House in the last session, and it is in many respects the end of a process that began a couple of years ago when the government initiated a wide ranging discussion on competition policy.
From my point of view, this legislation has appeared none too soon. I hope the bill will proceed to committee without lengthy debate and, in view of the fact that much discussion has already taken place on the general principles and philosophy of competition policy, that we can avoid the bill's being bogged down in committee as it is lobbied by one group or another over a lengthy period of time.
Of course, this is not to deny the right of interested parties to appear before the committee. But I am not anxious to be party to a procedure which sees the effective implementation of this bill delayed for a long period of time while many of those groups which have already had a substantial say in the formulation of the government's basic, philosophic approach come back to have another crack at it.
On many aspects of this bill I defer to the expertise of my learned friend from St. Paul's and associate myself with some of the caveats that he has entered against specific aspects of the bill. I would, however, most emphatically dissociate myself and my party from his views on the collective bargaining process and, I may say, from the views which he quoted as being those of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). In this respect I p.m afraid his bias got the better of his learning.
The organized labour movement will indeed be surprised to discover from my hon. friend that it is a monopoly, especially when organized strikebreaking is allowed to flourish across the country, not excluding in provinces governed by the same party to which my hon. friend from St. Paul's belongs. As far as I and my party are concerned, the fundamental premises of collective bargaining are inviolable.
I should like to comment upon some of the specific aspects of the bill which relate to its objective of creating an environment of fair play in the marketplace. We heard evidence before the committee on trends in food prices last year indicating that in that particular industry, as indeed in many others, such fair play was not currently being provided to consumers. In its survey of retail food stores published in November, 1973, the Food Prices Review Board drew specific attention to a number of practices. I had a look through that report to see to what extent their recommendations were reflected in this bill. For example,
March 13, 1974

the Food Prices Review Board drew attention to the practice known as double-ticketing. Let me quote from their report, page 7:
The practice of raising the price of a food product which is on the shelf of a store, and on which the price has already been marked, by restamping or adding another price label, is one to which consumers object strongly. It may well be that it is an accepted business practice to revalue inventories as prices change, but the practice of raising the price of food items in the store by double-ticketing is unacceptable to consumers.
I note that the bill accepts the recommendations of the review board to eliminate the practice of double-ticketing, but I also want to draw to the attention of the House the fact that the bill in no way interferes with-and I emphasize the words-the accepted business practice to revalue inventories as prices change. All that the bill does is to make it an offence, where two prices appear on an item, to sell the item at other than the lower price. But it takes no position on what I regard as the reprehensible policy of very many retail stores, of increasing the price of commodities already in inventory when the price of new shipments is increased. All this bill will do is to make the retail stores a little more efficient at changing labels; it will not solve the problem being faced by the consumer when inventory stock is increased to the price of new shipments.
Secondly, the Food Prices Review Board drew attention to what it refers to as the unavailable supplies of specials. The report states that many stores advertise weekly special prices for specific food products, and that although in some cases these specials are available in sufficient quantity to meet the demand, in many cases they are not. The bill deals in some respects with the problem but it does not really deal with the point emphasized by the board, that even where a store provides a so-called raincheck, some stores may adopt as a matter of policy the practice of not providing sufficient stocks of specials. Instead, they hand out rainchecks for the purpose of drawing customers back to the store on perhaps an unnecessary visit in the hope that when there they will purchase more than they would otherwise have done.
Other aspects of retail food practices which the board found unacceptable are misleading in-store practices like end-aisle displays, red lights over meat counters, hidden cash-register windows, misleading price signs, and so on. As the board said, these practices often confuse and deceive customers and it recommended specific action in each case, which so far as I have been able to make out is not reflected in specific provisions of this bill. Exaggerated price claims, proliferation of size in packaging, strengthening and bolstering of the inspection services of the department are all features of the Food Prices Review Board report which, again, so far as I have been able to make out are not included in the bill as it now stands.
While on the one hand, as I have said, I welcome the bill in a qualified way, I draw to the attention of the House that not even the limited range of practices which the Food Prices Review Board identified has been dealt with in the bill, and I therefore give notice to the minister of our intention to proceed in committee to move amendments to fill in the gaps.
Competition Bill
There are other features of this bill that perhaps are worthy of brief comment. I welcome efforts to broaden the provision under which action may be taken against misleading advertising and false marketing information. Here, again, I am of the opinion that these provisions require strengthening. I feel it is hightime the consumer was protected in a stronger way, not merely from deceitful statements in advertising but also from statements which create an impression or a broad representation that turns out not to be the case. I applaud the fact that the bill addresses itself to this problem.
Certain selling practices to which my hon. friend has referred, such as exclusive dealing and tied selling, are covered in the bill, and I welcome their inclusion as a logical and inevitable addition to the range of economic activities covered by the bill. I have some misgivings about that part of the bill dealing with extraterritoriality. As has already been mentioned, the implications of this problem have been brought home to us forcefully in the last couple of weeks in the case of MLW-Worthington Limited. I am not at all sure that the avenue being explored by the government in this bill to deal with the problem is adequate or is the best one, and I hope my colleague, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), will have something to say on that matter during this debate.
I cannot help but welcome the reference to and provisions to correct what the bill refers to as abuses against intellectual property. That is similar to occasions when the Liberal government steals an NDP program. Out of selfinterest, if for no other reason, I think that is a proper focus in the bill.
Certain features to protect small businesses-and I gather this is the principal purpose of their inclusion- such as refusal to deal provisions, consignment selling, exclusive dealing and otherwise, again at least begin to come to grips with the problems we heard much about in the food prices committee. There was a great deal of evidence to the effect that this was an important feature of the relationship between retailers and their wholesale distributors. The Food Prices Review Board in its February 28 review of bread prices had something to say on that matter and I quote from page 14 of their report:
The independent regional bakeries have found access to retail shelves limited or blocked by integrated or exclusive contractual arrangements between retail chains or groups and major bakeries.
Therefore, out of my interest in the matter of food prices, to say nothing of my concern for fair play in the marketplace, I again welcome the move the government is making in this direction. There is a provision in the bill, on which I do not propose to comment in detail, that deals with protection of athletes under certain conditions. It may be that my colleague, the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose), will have something to say on that matter.
There are one or two omissions I had hoped the government would deal with. One which has been referred to is the matter of class actions in which my colleague, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), has taken particular interest. Another is the vexing problem of what to do about loss leader selling. The minister indicated before the committee during the last session that the

March 13, 1974
Competition Bill
government did not intend to proceed at this time in respect of these matters, I gather because it had not made up its mind what policy to follow in this area. I would make the point that I suspect no blinding rays of inspiration are likely to strike the minister in the coming months and we might just as well deal with them now as later. Certainly in one area, where confectionery and tobacco distributors in eastern Canada have been affected by loss leader techniques of certain wholesale companies, real hardships have been created. I know this group hoped this bill would deal with this problem, as indeed I did too.
So much for a brief rundown of the bill itself. Let me now turn to some other aspects of the over-all problem. First of all, it seems to me that in passing a bill of this kind we are in a sense placing our trust in the effectiveness of the department, and the agencies which report to it, to implement the bill in an aggressive and effective way. I must say that my impression of the department has been that it is suffering from a severe case of tired blood, to put it as charitably as I can.
Let me give some examples. The bill refers to strengthening the powers of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission, but it is a fact, as has been adduced in the House recently, that this commission is understaffed and that the commission itself is minus most of its members; there have been vacancies for some time which the government has not moved to fill. I could not help but wonder why the government is moving to give more power and authority to that commission without at least providing it with a full complement of members. We give it new responsibilities in this bill, but there is no one there to carry out those responsibilities.
Looking through the report of the Auditor General for the fiscal year ending 1973, I noticed that the funds which were appropriated for the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission, which in that year totalled $248,000, were far from having been spent. While I do not wish to criticize the government for measures of economy, at the same time I cannot help reflect that a commission which began with a modest appropriation of one-quarter of a million dollars and which ended up spending only something like $100,000 is a commission which is not exactly burning out its bearings. I am led to the conclusion that there is a good deal of room for new energy and initiative in that area.
The minister admitted in the House recently that the department has been doing virtually nothing in the way of monitoring price movements. I can think of two examples, beef prices and steel prices. I know that is not central to this bill, but to me it is symptomatic of the lack of aggressiveness and concern by the minister on behalf of the consumers. The increase envisaged in the current estimates which have been tabled in this House for the combines investigation branch and the competition policy section of the minister's department is not reassuringly large compared with the remainder of the department. It would not appear to make any sense, having given the combines investigation branch and the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission new power under this bill, that we should not expect an increase in the way of costs.

Again, I do not want to criticize the government for saving the taxpayer's money, but I wonder how seriously the government intends to take the commitments which are implicit in this bill. This bill, and indeed the whole area of consumer affairs, requires an interventionist department and an interventionist minister. Can we reasonably expect this from that department and minister? On the basis of the performance so far, can we be sure that the government and the department are committed to take the muscular role on behalf of consumer which the minister has suggested in this House, and to stand behind the kind of commitment that is contained in the words of this bill?
I hope the minister, whose evasiveness is a byword in Parliament, will alter his performance in the coming weeks. We nead no more thrashing about as on the bread price issue. I refer, as well, to the curious new schedule the minister and the Prime Minister have announced in respect of the Food Prices Review Board. This does not reassure me, nor does the refusal of the government to say anything specific about the need to empower the minister, or his department, or the Food Prices Review Board, or a new prices review board, or any agency, to enforce the roll-back of prices when increases cannot be justified. The minister's refusal to do this leaves a question in my mind concerning whether the government is serious about its commitment.
There is in my party great skepticism concerning competition bills and policies. We worry whether these bills and policies are designed to lull the consumer into the assumption something is being done, while in fact no serious effort is being undertaken by the government to interfere with the traditional right of the business community of Canada to lay down the terms and conditions on which it will do business and to set prices as it sees fit.
At the core of any competition policy that seeks to come to grips with real problems lies the matter of market structure. Some kinds of market structure, such as those we can see in Canada, are the very antithesis of competition as the average person understands the term. There is the domination of an industry by one or a few companies, or the domination of one sector of the economy by a few dominant and related industry leaders. There is a good deal of evidence that this kind of industry domination, this oligopolistic domination, is the norm in the Canadian economy rather than the exception. I concede that the minister readily accepts that this bill in no way tackles that problem. Presumably the so-called phase two of the bill will do so.
However, let us not be under any illusion in this House that passage of this bill, with its useful measures, will in any serious way come to grips with the problem of domination of the economy by a relatively small number of corporate giants and the consequent problems which flow from that domination. Let me mention some aspects of the problem. There is the problem of administered prices which reflect not the cost of production but what the traffic will bear. When we come to the performance of Canadian companies in the past year, we do not have to look very far to see abnormally high profit levels, manipulation of supply, monopsonistic purchasing methods, and excess capacity. There are industry or sector common
March 13, 1974

fronts vis-a-vis the consumer, as we saw a few weeks ago with the bakeries. And there are those very unfair retailing practices with which this bill does deal.
If we did not have in this economy a prevalent condition of market domination and concentration, we would not have nearly so many instances of unfair treatment in the marketplace as we have today and much of the necessity for the bill would be obviated. It is true that market concentration does provide some economies of scale. That, of course, has been the traditional argument for concentration. However, we must ask ourselves whether the advantages which accrue from such concentration go to the firms, or to the consumer and whether the leverage of domination is being used against, and not for, the consumer.
In many instances the consumer does not enjoy any economies arising from large scale. I recognize that my allegations are broad, but I am sure any member who sat on the committee on food prices last year or who has dealt with the problem of competition over the years will recognize the force of my remarks. After all, what is the incentive to efficiency, low prices and public service, when competition is minimized and you can make your buck anyway? Our over-all policy objective, as we begin the process of establishing a so-called competition policy for Canada, surely must be to preserve the genuine economies of large scale and advantages which accrue from them and translate those into benefits for the public.
I have mentioned evidence of market concentration in Canada, some of which we heard before the food prices committee. I had hoped that committee would have been reconstituted in this session so that in that vitally important sector of the economy we might begin to hear evidence in a detailed and systematic way on the matter of concentration. I regret that my colleagues both in the Liberal and Conservative parties did not see fit to support my motion to recommend to the government that that committee be reconstituted.
The kind of concentration that I am talking about does not always result in criminal, premeditated collusion to which this bill and the Combines Investigation Act address themselves. What happens in so many cases is simply that there exists a tacit understanding that prices will be kept within recognized bounds, rather in the same way as one country manipulates its currency with regard to another. There is no collusion, no obvious premeditated interrelationship, but rather a general, tacit, unspoken but nonetheless effective agreement that competition per se will not be allowed to get out of hand.
We heard in the food prices committee about the so-called supermarket price war of three or four years ago and how the retail chain which initiated that earned the undying resentment of its competitors, what commotion its activities created within the retail food industry, and how grateful all the major supermarkets were when that kind of price competition was brought to an end and stability restored. By and large, it remains true today, and it does not really matter what supermarket you shop in, there is little difference in price and the price is always wrong.

speechtext: By gosh, it is.

speechtext:
A few years ago a royal commission in western Canada undertook an in-depth study of monopolistic grocery retail trade practices. I refer to the Batten report which concluded that there was indeed a high degree of concentration resulting in excess profits, excess capacity, self-cancelling and costly advertising campaigns and luxurious and expensive supermarkets. The report in fact calculated the cost of this to a family of four as being almost $120 a year. That is a high price to pay for concentration. The report said specifically that Canada Safeway and George Weston Ltd., possessed sufficient power to enable prices to rise above competitive levels. It recommended investigation under the Combines Investigation Act. There have been efforts to discredit the Batten report, but it is interesting to note that a recent ruling by the Alberta Supreme Court has ordered Canada Safeway to reduce its domination of retail grocery markets in Calgary and Edmonton.
In a speech made last year, as reported in the Financial Post, an advertising executive said the following when speaking to the Canadian grocery distributors institute meeting in Toronto:
So what's so bad about industry co-operation? After all, your competitors aren't your enemies but your consumers are.
I suggest that that kind of attitude is engendered and bred by the absence of any vital competition. If we take a look at the instance of concentration in the food industry-and I only give a few examples because I do not have a great deal of time left-we discover, for example, that in the breakfast cereal manufacturing industry the four largest plants account for 90 per cent of factory shipments. Sugar refineries account for 65 per cent of the four largest plants. In food retailing generally the four largest establishments account for 41 per cent of all the sales in Canada. In the slaughtering and meat processing industry, the four largest firms account for 58 per cent of the value of factory shipments. In flour milling, the top four firms account for almost 80 per cent of the value of factory shipments, and so the story goes.
Moving out of the food industry and taking a look at industry generally across Canada, we discover that in the pulp and paper industry the four largest enterprises account for 36 per cent of factory shipments. In newsprint mills, the four largest enterprises account for 44 per cent. In iron and steel mills, they account for 77 per cent. In steel pipe and tube mills-and we will need a lot of steel pipe in this country if we are going to build pipelines-the four largest firms control 78 per cent of factory shipments.
In motor vehicle manufacturing, a classic example, the top three or four firms account for 93 per cent. In cement manufacturing, a group recently in the news, the top four firms account for 77 per cent. In petroleum refineries, the top four companies account for 80 per cent of factory shipments; and among manufacturers of mixed fertilizers, about whom we will hear a good deal in the weeks to come, the top four companies account for 62 per cent of factory shipments.
These are all terribly important and positive sectors of the Canadian economy. As consumers and as builders of the Canadian economy, we will rely upon these manufac-

March 13, 1974
Competition Bill
turers and industries for supplies in certain vital areas in the years to come. I want this House to ask itself to what extent parliament and the government, to say nothing of the ordinary consumer, can be assured of fair treatment by the suppliers.
There has been evidence in recent weeks of certain companies being prosecuted under the Combines Investigation Act for activities in restraint of trade. The fact is that right now the Canadian people are terribly conscious of the fact that they cannot be certain, either at the retail level with which this bill deals, in areas of advertising with which this bill deals, or in the far more fundamental areas of the kind of structure under which this economy operates, that they are getting fair treatment in the marketplace. Until we deal, not merely with the provisions of this bill but with the whole area of the market structure, we will not have dealt with so-called competition policy.
This bill, rightly, deals with certain kinds of retail practices, certain types of wholesale transactions which go some way toward assuring a greater degree of fairness in the consumer marketplace, and this is important. But the bill really addresses itself to the result of lack of real competition and to the symptoms of the problem, rather than to its root causes.
The minister says he will be coming along within a year with the other three-quarters or 90 per cent of his competition policy. I think the minister would do well to reflect that a year is a long time in the life of this parliament, and that it would be in the best interests of all of us, not the least of whom are Canadian consumers, if he would hurry up the process. Let us get that phase two before the committee as soon as possible, particularly if my hon. friend wants to lead a large number of lobby and pressure groups by the hand before the committee, in which case we are going to need some time. That is just another reason why I think we should proceed.

The people of Canada have been putting up with a lot for a long time. This parliament has listened for a long time to the pros and cons of competition policy. I sometimes wonder what we are going to hear that is new. I am not interested in providing the louder voices with another opportunity to shout against the efforts of the Canadian consumer to get fair play in the Canadian marketplace.
I suggest, notwithstanding the interjection of my learned and hon. friend from St. Paul's that the separation of this stage of the competition policy from the more fundamental area of market concentration, although valid for the purposes of expediting discussion, is an artificial separation and ought not to be regarded as grounds for unduly delaying the introduction of the far more important sections which we yet await.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, ADMINISTRATION AND OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill introduced by the minister a few days ago and read for the first time in this House on March 11, Bill C-7, concerning

the combines and bank acts, is a most important bill and also fairly bulky.
This bill contains several technical amendments and we will have the opportunity of giving it further consideration in committee and in this House on third reading. Our party will have several amendments to propose. This bill is extremely important because it deals with mergers, monopolies, limitations of all types on trade and free competition, and with other matters vital to the Canadian consumer. I read all the amendments contained in this bill and it reminds me of a gardener in the spring who finds that his tree is diseased, that some of its branches are dried out, that there is something wrong with it, and decides to water it when it is the roots that are diseased.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) wants to deal with the problem of mergers, combines, by looking after the branches when our economic system is ill.
Mr. Speaker, there are, on the other hand, some interesting points and before going into the crux of the matter, I should like to say to the minister that some amendments are valid, for example, those dealing with misleading advertising, misrepresentations made by salesmen or retailers when selling their products and also misleading or invalid warranties or guarantees when the products are sold to the consumer. Those are the three items which I consider extremely worthwhile.
I think, however, that the more important amendments are those dealing with competition. I do not find in this bill valid amendments which could alter the fact that in Canada monopolies are still in control. The elimination of competition, Mr. Speaker, is extremely detrimental economically to the consumer. For years we have objected to American or foreign companies coming to Canada to develop our natural resources. When we object to those foreign companies developing our natural resources, Mr. Speaker, I think it is not enough to expose them, we must have legislation that would then allow Canadians or Canadian companies to develop, here in Canada, our natural resources. I have absolutely nothing against foreign companies. If they settled in Canada, it is because we did not develop our natural resources. We have been unable to shape a policy to allow us to benefit from our own wealth without resorting to foreign capital.
Mr. Speaker, that is why it was proposed to do away with the elements which made competition impossible until now because the production or distribution of our goods were in the hands of monopolies, we have never been able to suggest positive solutions. We have heard much that is negative until now, but few positive suggestions that would allow the Canadian economy to be developed by Canadians in Canada. Even now, we are studying a bill that advocates a negative solution to that problem which has always existed.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to define the distinction we, Social Crediters, make between private enterprise and monopolies.
The Social Crediters have always been against monopolies, but they are in favour of private enterprise.
Some of our socialist friends take pleasure in confusing "private enterprise" and "monopoly". Free enterprise must
March 13, 1974

be denounced and means should be taken to make it powerless. We are in favour of private enterprise but not of free enterprise.
Free enterprise enables a group to control the market in a given area. Free enterprise is not private enterprise.
Some companies in Canada are no longer private enterprises because they have no more competition. Those, in our view, are actually monopolies and that is why Social Crediters are opposed to free enterprise, monopoly; they are in favour of private enterprise.
That is why Social Crediters have always wholeheartedly supported private enterprise in Canada and why we denounce free enterprise at times. Free enterprise and private enterprise are two different things.
So, in the proposals, recommendations, suggestions that we make on various bills introduced in the House, we advocate an economic system based on private enterprise and not on free enterprise or, in other words, monopolies.
Through this bill, the minister meant to put teeth in the Combines Investigation Act. He has incorporated into this bill some positive political measures, but such measures without the adoption of positive economic measures at the same time does not solve anything at all. If we pass positive political measures which are not supported by economic measures enabling individuals to compete against monopolies, we will remain in the clutches of monopolies, mergers and combines, which will have to pay fines, but according to the figures quoted today, less than 1 per cent of the profits made by monopolies have been subjected to a fine.
The measures that the minister has included in this bill deal especially with the small businessmen who will be subject to this bill like anybody else, but they will have no effect on the multinational companies.
How can this bill bring about a change? What can bill C-7 do against multinational companies which are now increasing overnight all prices at the same time, invoking the false pretext of the oil and gas shortage? Under such a bill, the minister cannot act against the multinational companies which hold sway over our economy. The only thing he can do is to fine them $2,000 or $5,000, a ridiculous amount for them which is tax deductible.
What shocked me about this bill, Mr. Speaker, is to note that the government is trying to punish and restrain everybody. However, at the same time, banks are given special privileges.
Mr. Speaker, as we have always said, the banks are the basis of the existing monopoly which controls the others. According to its whim, the monopoly of money and credit can create a monopoly of production or destroy it. And when I hear people who strongly denounce monopolies, and rightly so, in such and such a sector of industry, and yet, refrain from attacking the very monopoly which creates all the others, I feel they fall short of the target. They go only after the small fry, overlooking the villain who will go on with his dirty work.
Mr. Speaker, the bill under consideration will enable us to look after the sick while allowing the disease to spread. The hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) referred
Competition Bill
earlier to a US firm in Montreal which recently sold locomotives to Cuba, something it could not do in the United States because of the American embargo on Cuba. This same firm located in Montreal, imposes on its competitors a 210 day waiting period for the delivery of the parts required to repair Diesel engines and locomotives thus compelling big industrialists who own locomotives with Diesel or other engines, to go to this one company in Montreal which has the parts on hand. This means that this firm has the monopoly of repairs and maintenance, that no one will dare compete with it because its competitors must wait 210 days for the delivery of parts. Yet, even the National Harbours Board, with Diesel engines in need of repair must go to this American firm if it wants quick repair or delivery and pay the price asked.
Mr. Speaker, what is this bill going to change in respect of this American company which exerts a monopoly on parts and delivers them to its competitors when it is good and ready, thereby compelling users of heavy machinery to do business with it.
Mr. Speaker, in the speech he delivered on January 24, 1974, to the County York Law Association of Toronto, the minister said on page 8, and I quote: "Among those practices, there is the refusal to sell, the consignment sale, the exclusive rights, binding sales, market restriction".
Mr. Speaker, I do not see anything in this bill that will prevent that American company in Montreal to restrict the market or to impose exclusive rights. In fact, it presently has the exclusivity of the market, with no competitors or no other company to take its place. There is another thing that struck me in the Royal Commission report: from 1972 to 1973, there have been 188 inquiries, i.e. 100 less than in 1971-72. And of the 3,470 cases that were studied, in only 68 cases a verdict of guilty was brought in. But of those companies found guilty, most have not yet paid their fines.
Let me now quote from an article by a company accountant, published in the Globe and Mail issue of Tuesday, March 12, 1974, page 5:

A fine of $150,000 against Ocean Construction would be comparable to a fine of $750 against an individual earning $50,000. The same fine against Canada Cement Lafarge would be comparable to a fine of $130.63 against the same individual.
Mr. Speaker, the present Combines Investigation Act is inefficient. Nothing in the wording of this bill proves that we will be able to apply it without going back to the source. In our economic policy, we have not developped any means designed to encourage private enterprise in Canada, to help the individual to compete with large companies, to maintain and control free enterprise. We want to assist private enterprise in Canada, but we want to do it with positive means and not negative legislation so as to enable private enterprise to compete with free enterprise in Canada.
I have here a letter dated November 2, 1973, which appeared in the National Association of Tobacco. The second paragraph states and I quote:

March 13, 1974
Competition Bill
Our group is very concerned by our federal government's lack of interest and shortsightedness as regards certain deficiencies of the Combines Act. Ever since its implementation, businessmen throughout Canada have challenged Section 34 of the Act and predict what would happen if no change was brought about. Their predictions have now come true but we are still doing nothing to bring about the necessary changes. The serious dangers anticipated for small business are now reaching their highest point and they will soon have reached the point of no return. Therefore, we ask that this matter be raised in the House during this session and that a solution be found in the next few months.
Mr. Speaker, as I said in this House, on March 1, 1974, we are living in an economic system where production is in the hands of a very small group. At present, economic organizations have absolute control over a given type of production. Me. Speaker, whatever regulations we may pass, as long as there is no competition between producers to enable them to dispose of their own production, without having to go through monopolies of distribution, Mr. Speaker, no anti-combines legislation will be efficient. We keep going around in a circle and we shall never get any results.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, the Social Crediters maintain that we should put into effect a consumer policy thus making production available to consumers. We must put forward a policy designed to finance production so that producers may control it entirely thus escaping the control of any monopoly which may exist between production and consumption.
This is why it is utterly silly and inconsistent to speak of nationalization, government control, socialization, of putting everything in the hands of the government, of public concerns, of multinational corporations or cartels. It does not make any sense at all. Why? Because in an exclusive system of production there are people-and we know some in Quebec and everywhere else in Canada- who lay down the law. They challenge it, they pay fines and do not fear convictions. They are then exclusive agents, masters of both consumers and producers.
Mr. Speaker, with regard to private enterprise, concrete legislation is needed at all costs to bring it to heel. My hon. friends from the NDP do not seem to make any distinction between private enterprise and free enterprise. That is why from time to time they wonder if we are socialists when we expose monopolies, combines, multinational corporations which have exclusive power over a given production.
We use roughly the same terms as they do but we do not want to replace a multinational enterprise by a state enterprise as they want to do because when we create a state enterprise it hides behind bureaucracy and legislation. With the principle I put forward and which we already stated in this House on March 1, 1974, we will allow producers to become independent from multinational corporations, combines and those who now have the economic power.
Mr. Speaker, once again, we do not see anything in this bill. Wider powers are given to those who hold the monopoly over creation of credit. There is no reference to the ten chartered banks in Canada which have the power to create an economic crisis or prosperity in this country tomorrow morning.

A good friend of mine was telling me recently that he once borrowed $240,000 from the Industrial Development Bank, made all his payments and cleared his debt. He had become even more solvent than he was when he borrowed in the first place. And now he has not yet received approval for a loan of $30,000. The thing has been dragging on for six months. That means that banks are now creating a climate of economic crisis and if tomorrow morning they want to start a crisis in Canada this Bill C-7 will be of no use whatsoever because it does not deal with the control and creation of money.
Small combines, trust companies, those that own billions of dollars in assets are exposed but not those that make billions, that create billions as banks can do.
The greatest monopoly of all is the monopoly of credit, of that money which is reserved exclusively for banks. Six years ago, a U.S. Senate committee of inquiry was instructed to investigate combines and monopolies in the United States. When the chairman of the committee made public the inquiry report, he said: There is only one monopoly in the United States, and that is the monopoly of credit, for it is the one that breeds all the others.
Mr. Speaker, Social Crediters have often denounced this in the House. We want the Bank of Canada, the bank of the people, which is our institution and our financial organization, to be the one authorized to give credit to Canadians when they need it. We do not want the banks to retain this power they now have. Banks should be business institutions that accept deposits and lend the depositors' money, institutions in the money business that have a right to make profits. But banks should not have the monopoly to make this kind of money called "credit money".
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the minister is quite convinced that his bill will make tremendous reforms in our combines system, our monopoly system, but it will affect only the small businesses, not the big ones, for the latter are quite able to dodge the regulations, just like banks will manage to evade the bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre De Bane (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer And Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, ADMINISTRATION AND OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to take part in this debate as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray), and all the more so because this is one of the most important and progressive pieces of legislation this government has introduced since it has come to power.
Indeed, the purpose of this bill is to maximize human and capital resources, so that the whole Canadian economy and all Canadians, consumers as well as producers, can benefit from it.
Indeed, the policy on competition is one of the basic elements of policy on commerce and because of this, its complexity and its scope, the minister has introduced this bill as a first step in an in-depth revision of the various measures that bear, directly or indirectly, on the whole field of competition.
Hon. members will recall that in 1966, the Liberal government asked the Economic Council of Canada for an
March 13, 1974

in-depth study on that matter. In 1971, the present Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) introduced Bill C-256 which gave rise to virulent debates through the country and when the present minister was invested with this portfolio he decided to conduct an in-depth study, step by step, in that field.
Recently I heard the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) criticize some alleged shortcomings of that bill. I was listening with all the more suspicion because I remembered that the last review of the Combines Investigation Act had been made under the last Progressive Conservative administration in 1960.
And what happened in 1960 when the Progressive Conservative government decided to amend the Combines Investigation Act? I wish to quote an article by Queen's University Professor H. G. Thorburn, in a book entitled he systeme politique du Canada published by the University of Ottawa in 1970 under the direction of Mr. Louis Sabourin.
In this article, Professor Thorburn declares at page 217, and I quote:
When the Conservative party gained power in 1957 after 22 years in opposition, it did not feel at all bound by the combines legislation passed under the Liberals. The Conservative government announced that the act was going to be revised, encouraging everyone concerned to make representations. Two years later, the Conservatives introduced their bill in the House of Commons. The bill was aimed at meeting the requirements of the financial world.
And I quote now from page 219:
Voluminous briefs were submitted by commercial associations representing the interests of large businesses. They included amendment proposals which were obviously aimed at blunting the teeth of the legislation-
Since the government bill was largely a favourable answer to the demands of businessmen, it was normal that consumers, farmers, and workers organizations, which were all dissatisfied with it, appealed against it. However, the legislation was written in such technical terms that several groups that would reasonably be against the bill, considered they did not have the expertise to assert their objections. However, the Canadian Consumer Association, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture... were outrightly opposed, with the support of some economists and political scientists.
On the subject of economists, the professor says, and I quote:
They were the only group not representing a large sector of the population. On one hand, they possessed unequaled competence and were obviously disinterested. Personnally, they stood to gain nothing in this matter, whatever the outcome, except as average citizens. Economists were therefore unanimous in their opposition to the bill. In all, twenty-eight economists and five political scientists made their opinion known to government. ... They made very serious representations and their analysis was also supported by highly technical demonstrations. Their conclusion, however, was clear and unanimous.
One economist even stated that the amendments were meant to undermine the effectiveness of the steps taken by the Canadian government against combines, since it would become much more difficult to lodge successful legal proceedings.
Mr. Speaker, this is how some economists in 1960 considered the planned revision of the competition policy advocated by the then Conservative government. They unanimously rejected it to say nothing of the Canadian Consumers Association and other groups which I mentioned a while ago.
When the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) wants to point out some deficiencies, we must listen with much misgivings, since the policy followed by the official oppo-
Competition Bill
sition when it was in power gave rise to the objections to Canadian consumer groups and all the economists who then submitted briefs to the committee.
I quoted a study by a Queen's University professor, one who is uncommitted, in order to prove how we took a step backward in 1960, on account of a Conservative government.
I was saying at the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, how proud I am to take part in this debate because the bill introduced by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray), is a very ambitious one, not because of the various phases that will follow but because of its very substance. Indeed, it takes the form of an amendment to the Combines Investigation Act and not that of a replacement. Therefore this part of the government program to modernize the legislation on competition will be easier to administer and will come into force more quickly since it will be based on the process and the machinery related to the Combines Investigation Act.
Since the bill constitutes a set of amendments, the jurisprudence which will accrue from it will of course still be useful, except to the extent that amendments will make some parts obsolete. In other words, the practitioner who will be called upon to make a decision about the enforcement of the legislation will be on rather familiar grounds.
Some people are wondering what makes a bill such as this so important. In that regard, I would like to read a paragraph from page 8 of the 1969 report of the Economic Council of Canada, and I quote:
It would be wrong, however, to leave the impression that the consequences for efficiency of a relative absence of competitive pressure are invariably an esoteric matter, beyond the capacity of an ordinary intelligent person to discern. As everyday observation will confirm, lack of strong competition in a company's product market increases the risk of sloppiness, poor use of productive resources, and excessive production and distribution costs. An environment is created in which both waste and a comfortable, if not necessarily spectacular, profit margin can persist, undisturbed by clear and urgent signals from the market.
This brings us to a fundamental tenet relating to competition policy. The institution and maintenance of a competition policy such as presently exists in Canada may be taken to reflect a belief that, over the greater part of the economy, competitive marker forces are potentially capable of allocating resources better and more cheaply, with a less cumbersome administrative overhead, than any alternative arrangement such as wholesale public ownership and control, detailed government regulation of enterprise, or self-regulation by large industrial units within a corporate state.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, a competition policy is extremely important since it enables all Canadians to share the wealth of the country and obtain the best products at the lowest price possible.
What are the various points covered by that essential bill? Obviously, as the minister stated earlier, the first is:
(a)	A series of prohibitions on specific commercial practices prejudicial to the consumer's interests. Those provisions provide criminal offences or bring desirable amendments to existing prohibitions as follows:
(1)	The provisions of the present bill dealing with misleading advertising are altered and made clearer to apply to all kinds of false statements made to the public about products and services rather than only to printed material.

March 13, 1974
Competition Bill
If the bill is passed, as I hope, the general impression of statements as much as their literal meaning will be taken into account.
(2)	false or misleading guarantees or warranties are forbidden.
(3)	any sale at any price that exceeds the lowest of two or more prices is forbidden in the case of goods with double ticketing.
(4)	pyramid sales are forbidden within limitations and referral sales as defined are forbidden,
(5)	bait and switch and replacement sales are forbidden,
(6)	sales above advertized prices are forbidden,
(7)	promotional contests are forbidden subject to certain rules,
(8)	the prohibition of resale pricing is strengthened.
And, Mr. Speaker, I only touched on one of the aspects
of this bill now before hon. members. I could go through everyone of those points on misleading advertizing. We now know how we are going to be able to get more readily to those who want to go around the market rules, the area of warranty, list all possible cases where to comply with the act warranties will have to be other things than misrepresentations beyond the safeguards of civil law.
Another thing contained in this bill introduced by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) is that from now on,
(b)	Upon a request from the Director of Investigation and Research the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission may
(1)	examine cases of refusal to sell and after giving the supplier every opportunity to make his case, order him to supply his customers or recommend tariff changes;
(2)	still upon request from the Director of Investigation and Research-
(2)	examine cases where consignment sales were used to control the prices of a dealer or set price differentials between competitors and after giving the supplier every opportunity to make his case, order him to cease that practice;
(3)	to review cases where exclusiveness, that is to say to demand that a buyer only trades in a few specific products, is practiced by large suppliers in order to substantially limit competition and, after giving suppliers reasonable opportunities of being heard, to issue the necessary order;
The Commission, when requested by the Director of investigations and research, is authorized:
(4)	to review cases where tied selling, that is to say the sale of a product tied to the sale of another, are practiced by large suppliers in order to substantially limit competition and, after giving the suppliers reasonable opportunities of being heard, to issue the necessary order.
(5)	The Commission is authorized to review cases where the market restriction, that is to say when the supplier, as selling condition, imposes restrictions as regards the market where his customer may carry on his business, is practiced by large suppliers in order to substantially limit competition and, after giving the suppliers reasonable opportunities of being heard, to issue the necessary order.

And finally, the Commission, when requested by the director of investigations, is authorized
(6)	to examine cases where foreign judgments, laws or directives from foreign directors are found to be contrary to the public interest and after having afforded people concerned a reasonable opportunity to be heard, to issue orders to forbid their implementation in Canada.
Here is something else, Mr. Speaker, concerning this extremely important bill, namely:
(c)	legal prohibitions as to interest associations, mergers and monopolies limiting themselves mainly to articles and staple production and trade, are more far reaching and concern all services and industries that supply services.
As hon. members know, this is a major change that does not concern services but only the supplying or sale of articles. Service provision represents a more and more important part of the Canadian gross national product, and it was only normal for the government to include from now on certain aspects of the service sector in the field that is covered by the legislation. I continue:
(c)	... According to the already well-established jurisprudence, prohibitions under the law do not apply to restrictive trade practices expressly authorized under present federal or provincial legislation.
Of course in some sectors the market is controlled, and it is not our intention either to disturb certain practices that are not meant to be prejudicial to the market system in Canada.
In another field, it is said that:
(d)	it is clearly stated that for a restrictive agreement to be considered as contrary to the law because it unduly reduces competition, it is not necessary to prove that its effect would be to remove all or almost all competition.
As we know, the Supreme Court recently interpreted agreements to reduce competition. It forbids only those which would eliminate all competition.
And again:
(e)	According to the bill, the following practices become new offences:
(1)	a company established in Canada cannot apply guidelines coming from abroad implementing an agreement which is against this legislation;
(2)	offer rigging;
(3)	unreasonable agreements on participation in amateur and professional sport;
(4)	failure to comply with an order of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission will become in itself an offence in the future.
Another subject covered by this bill is specified in the following clause:
(f)	Provisions are included to authorize and facilitate civil prosecutions to recover the loss or damage resulting from a conduct which is against the act, up to the total sum in question, plus the cost of the inquiry and of the prosecution.
This is, in my opinion, a measure that the present government is very courageous to put forward and it will
March 13, 1974

greatly contribute to the stabilization of the market system in the country.
Here is another important clause:
(g)	Clause 32(2) already stipulates that a court cannot hand down a conviction if it is established that an agreement relates only to some particular questions. These questions are complemented by agreements on the size or on the shape of containers, the adoption of the metric system and measures for the protection of the environment.
The bill also includes new proposals providing for the presentation, when the proof is made, of non-confidential
Competition Bill
official statistics and it indicates how they should be prepared and presented.
Mr. Speaker, I did not deal with all subjects covered in this bill but I think I did mention enough to show hon. members that the legislation introduced by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) should be supported unanimously by all members who have at heart the promotion and progress of the Canadian economy.
